Foster

FOSS-ter -- two syllables, stress on the first syllable, FOSS. · verb

Hear It

What It Means

To foster encourage the development of something.

The mentorship program pairs new hires with veterans to foster confidence during the first year.

Worked Example

The librarian sets out puzzles by the window, hosts a build-your-own-comic club, and lets kids vote on new books -- and within a year, twice as many students spend their lunch period reading.

The librarian's small efforts foster a reading culture -- they encourage it to grow. To foster something is to nourish and encourage its development: you create the right conditions and tend them until the thing flourishes.

How Foster Sits Among Its Neighbors

Synonyms — open each to see how it differs

nurture

nurture: care for and help something grow

cultivate

cultivate: develop something by attention and effort

promote

promote: actively support the progress of something

Antonyms

hinder

hinder: hold back the development of something

suppress

suppress: prevent something from growing or being expressed

How Strong Is It? — nurture → promote → foster

nurture vs. foster

nurture vs. foster: Nurture is hands-on and close, while foster works at arm's length -- a parent nurtures a child directly, but a city fosters the arts by building the theaters and funding the grants that let them grow.

promote vs. foster

promote vs. foster: Promote is louder than foster: to promote a cause is to push it publicly, while to foster it is quieter -- creating the conditions in which it can take root and grow on its own.

Build the Word

The pieces

root — fostor-

root — fostor-: food, nourishment (Old English fostor)

Put it together

Put it together: Foster is Old English fostor, 'food, nourishment' -- to foster a child was literally to feed and rear one. The nourishing idea survives in every modern use: to foster a talent, a friendship, or a love of science is to feed it until it can thrive on its own.

Where it comes from

Where it comes from: The root fostor meant food itself, so to foster someone was originally to do something very concrete: put meals in front of them. That literal feeding later stretched to anything a person can 'feed' and help grow.

Strength Check

Word Choice

Foster takes growing things as its object: foster creativity, foster trust, foster a love of music, foster economic growth. It implies patient encouragement over time rather than a single push. It also keeps its literal family sense -- a foster family takes in and cares for a child.
